title: Girls knocking before dawn
hookLine: girls knocking on doors in the dark, waking each other up
carry: satsang: we go to krishna together

cards: It's still dark, cold enough that nobody wants to leave the blanket. A group of girls goes from house to house, rapping on doors and calling through windows to friends still asleep. Get up.
The birds are already talking. You said you'd come. Are you deaf, or just pretending?
This isn't a diary. It's a poem: Andal's song cycle, the Tiruppavai.

teach.b: The Tiruppavai is set in the Tamil month of Margazhi, in the cold season. Andal imagines herself as one of the cowherd girls of Krishna's village, the same village we just left in the Bhagavata.
The girls have taken a vow for the month: rise before dawn, bathe, keep simple, and go together to seek him. So the songs move like a morning. First they gather.

Then they wake the girls who overslept, door by door, affectionate and funny, the way friends really talk. They arrive at the house of Nanda, Krishna's foster father. They wake the doorkeeper, then the family inside.
At last they stand before Krishna and tell him why they've come. On the surface, for a drum, a ritual drum for their vow. Then the songs turn.
The drum was an excuse. What they want is to belong to him, to serve him, not just today but in every life to come. Notice who's seeking here.

Not a lone hermit in a cave: a gang of friends dragging each other out of bed, refusing to go without the one still asleep. Hindus have a word for this: satsang, the company of people turned toward God.
In Andal's picture, nobody gets to the door alone, and nobody's left behind for being lazy.

teach.h: NOT A DRUM, BUT TO BELONG TO HIM.

teach.b: That's why these songs aren't only read. In Margazhi, people in Tamil homes and temples sing them before sunrise, together. A poem about waking each other up became a reason to get up.

how: During the Tamil month of Margazhi, Andal's Tiruppavai is sung before dawn in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes, and the day's verse is often recited in morning worship.

s: the Tiruppavai is a song about a lone hermit's prayer
it's a group of girls waking each other to go to Krishna together.
in the songs, Andal pictures herself as a cowherd girl of Krishna's village
she joins the girls of the village we met in the Bhagavata.
in the end, the drum is all the girls want
the songs turn: they want to belong to him in every life.

games.q: you're one of the girls. it's dark and cold, and one friend who promised to come is still asleep. what do you do?
o: go on without her; she had her chance.
knock and call and tease until she gets up.
games.why: the songs go door to door, teasing and calling the sleepers. in Andal's poem the vow is kept together: nobody goes to Krishna alone.

practice: Bring to mind one person who once woke you up, not with an alarm, but by knocking and calling until you didn't sleep through something that mattered.
Then think of someone you might knock for: a friend to bring to the temple, a cousin to sing with, someone to pray beside. That's satsang.
If you pray, hold them both before God in words you already use; if you don't, send one of them a message today.

wordCard.voice: The Alvars. The Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu. Andal is the one who wrote the Tiruppavai, girls waking each other before dawn to go and find Krishna.

orig.note: Tamil: the name of Andal's song cycle, sung before dawn in the month of Margazhi.
